modules.title: Magnetic pressure, thick-solenoid fields, stored energy and winding stresses
modules.answers: What field a pressure needs, and what that field does to the coil that makes it.
relations: Magnetic pressure: P = B²/(2μ₀); with field on both sides of a wall, P = (B_out² − B_in²)/(2μ₀)
Central field of a uniform-current thick solenoid (Montgomery): B₀ = μ₀ J a₁ β ln[(α + √(α² + β²)) / (1 + √(1 + β²))], α = a₂/a₁, β = L/(2a₁)
Stored energy of a long coil: E = (B₀²/2μ₀) π L [a₁² + 2Δ(a₂/3 − Δ/4)]
Hoop stress of a free turn: σ(r) = r J B(r); its maximum never falls below P/2, however thick the winding
Virial bound on structural mass: M ≥ ρE/σ
limits: Non-magnetic media. The on-axis field is exact for a uniform current density.
The field profile in the winding, the stored energy and the stresses use the long-coil approximation, good to about 10 % for β ≥ 3.
Each turn carries its own Lorentz load (no radial load sharing), which is an upper bound on the peak stress of a bonded winding.

modules.title: Off-axis field of a thick solenoid and the pressure it really puts on a workpiece
modules.answers: What the field is away from the axis, and how the pressure is really spread over a workpiece.
relations: Field of a circular loop from the complete elliptic integrals K and E (arithmetic-geometric mean)
Winding field: B(r, z) = J ∬ b_loop dA over the winding cross-section, with a mesh that grades towards the field point
Radial field, reduced exactly to one dimension: B_r = J ∫ [a_φ(a; r, z − L/2) − a_φ(a; r, z + L/2)] da
Perfectly conducting workpiece: ψ_coil + Σ G_ij I_j = 0 on every surface panel; then B_surface = μ₀|K| and P = B²/(2μ₀)
limits: Axisymmetric, non-magnetic and quasi-static, with a uniform winding current density.
The workpiece is a perfect conductor that was field-free before the pulse: skin depth much smaller than the part and the gap, pulse much shorter than the flux-diffusion time.
A sharp edge gives a mesh-dependent pressure peak. Give real parts their corner radius.
Checked against two closed forms: Montgomery's on-axis field, and the 3/2 B₀ equatorial field of a conducting sphere in a uniform field.

modules.title: REBCO conductor, carbon-nanosheet (CNS) reinforced winding, and pulsed-operation limits
modules.answers: Whether a REBCO winding can carry the current, hold the load and survive being pulsed.
relations: Engineering critical current density: J_e = J_e,sf g(T) (1 + B/B₀)^(−α) max(0, 1 − B/B_irr(T))
Iso-strain winding composite: E_c = Σ f_i E_i, allowed stress = E_c ε_lim with ε_lim = 0.4 % (REBCO)
Required modulus: E ≥ SF σ/ε_lim, which is 1 TPa at 4 GPa and 0.4 %
Loss per pulse: critical-state hysteresis (thin strip and Bean slab) plus copper eddy loss (dB/dt)² d² 2t/(12ρ)
Quench test: loss per pulse against the enthalpy from the operating temperature to the current-sharing temperature
limits: J_e is a parametric fit representative of 2020s commercial tape, calibrated at 4.2 K on data to 31 T. Above 31 T it is an extrapolation.
The rule of mixtures assumes continuous constituents aligned with the hoop direction and no thermal pre-strain.
Pulse losses are adiabatic and leave out the transport current, so they are lower estimates.

modules.title: Pulse-power network: capacitor banks, rotating machines and the coil they drive
modules.answers: What power supply the pulse needs: voltage, current, power, bank size and coil heating.
relations: Quarter-period law: ω₀ = π/(2 t_rise), V₀ I_pk = πE/t_rise, peak power = πE/(2 t_rise)
Turns trade current against voltage: L ∝ N², I ∝ 1/N, V₀ ∝ N
Series RLC discharge in all three damping regimes; the bank must hold E_field exp(R t_rise/L)
A homopolar rotor is a capacitor: C_eq = J/k² with k = V/ω
Conductor heating from the action integral ∫J² dt, starting at 77 K
Energy transfer between uncoupled inductors: at most 25 %
limits: A lumped circuit: no transmission-line effects, switch physics or coupling to the workpiece.
Coil stresses are handled by magnetics, conductor and containment.
Heating uses a linear resistivity law and a constant specific heat without magnetoresistance, so it is a lower estimate.

modules.title: Electromagnetic (magnetic-pulse) forming: eddy currents, field diffusion, skin heating and rigid-plastic tube compression
modules.answers: How a pulsed field loads, heats and moves a metal workpiece.
relations: Skin depth: δ = √(ρ/(π f μ₀))
Interior field of a shell: dB_in/dt = (B_out − B_in)/τ, τ = μ₀ a h/(2ρ); pressure P = (B_out² − B_in²)/(2μ₀)
Skin heating: ΔT = κ B²/(2μ₀ ρ_m c_p), whatever the pulse length (κ = 1 is the lower estimate, up to 2.4 at the surface)
Magnetic diffusion into a heating slab: ∂B/∂t = ∂/∂z[(ρ(T)/μ₀) ∂B/∂z], Crank-Nicolson
Rigid-plastic tube: m dv/dt = −(P_net − k σ h/r), with the trapped flux compressed as B_in r² = const
limits: A solid, non-magnetic (saturated) workpiece: a long thin shell in a uniform axial field.
The lumped shell model assumes the current is uniform through the wall. For a wall thicker than the skin depth the skin estimate applies to the surface.
Adiabatic. Solid-phase properties are extrapolated above the melting point and latent heat is ignored.
The tube model has no elastic rebound and no buckling.

modules.title: Flow stress, forging pressure, adiabatic heating and forgeability of metals
modules.answers: Whether a given pressure can deform a given metal, and what limits the deformation.
relations: Johnson-Cook: σ = (A + B εⁿ)(1 + C ln(ε̇/ε̇₀))(1 − T*ᵐ)
Zerilli-Armstrong (bcc): σ = c₀ + c₁ exp(−c₃T + c₄T ln ε̇) + c₅ εⁿ
Forging pressure: p = Q σ (1 + μ d/(3h)), with Q from 1 (uniaxial) to about 3 (indentation)
Adiabatic heating: dT = f β σ dε/(ρ c_p), β = 0.9
Culver instability: dσ/dε = 0 along the adiabatic path
limits: Each published fit holds only inside its recorded strain-rate and temperature window. The assessment says when it is extrapolating.
Materials without a published fit use a Hollomon power law from tensile data with an assumed rate sensitivity.
Bulk, uniform deformation. Hydrostatic pressure alone changes no shape, so a die, a mandrel or a free surface is assumed.
The recorded ductile-brittle transition temperatures are quasi-static values.

modules.title: Microstructure after a cold, fast magnetic forming pulse: dislocations, grains and heat
modules.answers: What a cold, fast forming pulse leaves behind in the grains.
relations: Taylor hardening: Δσ = M α G b (√ρ − √ρ₀)
Dislocation cell size: d = K/√ρ, K about 10
Hall-Petch: σ_y = σ₀ + k d^(−1/2)
Grain refinement with strain: d = d_sat + (d₀ − d_sat) exp(−ε)

Skin exposure: ΔT = κ B²/(2μ₀ ρ c_p), held for about (δ/2)²/α_thermal
limits: Scaling laws with estimated constants (Taylor α 0.2 to 0.5, cell constant 10 to 20, recrystallisation anchor 0.3 to 0.5 T_m). Results are order-of-magnitude estimates.
Fracture toughness and fatigue life are not modelled.
Twinning, texture, recovery, grain growth and phase transformations are not modelled.

Linear fits are used inside their recorded pressure range. A phase transition is a low branch, a mixed-phase plateau and a high branch.
The drive pressure is constant during the flight, so flyer velocities are upper bounds.

modules.title: Impact (magnetic-pulse) welding of dissimilar metals: the weldability window
modules.answers: Which impact conditions weld two metals, and what drive pressure reaches them.
relations: Collision point: V_c = V_p/sin β
Lower (bonding) limit: V_p,min = k √(HV/ρ), k from 0.6 to 1.2
Jetting limit: V_c below the bulk sound speed of both metals
Upper (melting) limit, Wittman: V_p,max = (1/N) √(T_m c₀) (κ c_p c₀/(ρ h))^(1/4) / V_c
Wavy interface above a collision Reynolds number (ρ_f + ρ_t) V_c²/(2(HV_f + HV_t)) of about 10.6
Interdiffusion: x = √(2Dt), D = D₀ exp(−Q/RT)
limits: The window limits are empirical correlations calibrated on explosive welding of similar metals. For dissimilar pairs their constants are uncertain by tens of per cent.
The collision angle is an input. It is not solved from the flyer's deformation.
Interface heating, melt layer and diffusion figures are order-of-magnitude estimates.

modules.title: Pore closure and densification: can a magnetic pressure pulse make "zero-porosity" parts?
modules.answers: Whether pressure alone closes internal pores, and whether closing them heals them.
relations: Collapse threshold of an isolated pore: P = (2/3) σ ln(1/f)
Residual porosity: f = min(f₀, exp(−3P/(2σ)))
Trapped gas: f = f₀ p₀/P
Inertial collapse time (Rayleigh): t = 0.915 a √(ρ/ΔP)
Diffusion bonding: t ≈ L²/D, D = D₀ exp(−Q/RT)
Powder yielding (Helle, Easterling and Ashby): P = 3D²(D − D₀)/(1 − D₀) σ_y below 90 % density, (2/3) σ_y ln(1/(1 − D)) above
limits: Isolated spherical pores in a rigid, perfectly plastic matrix at its yield stress, so the thresholds are lower bounds on the pressure for full closure.
Creep is not modelled. Hot isostatic pressing enters as a cited benchmark, not as a model result.
Pressures are mechanical pressures already delivered to the part. There is no field solver for complex shapes here.
Bonding uses volume self-diffusion with an estimated prefactor.

modules.answers: What wall contains a given pressure, and what launchers and fusion coils actually ask of it.
relations: Lamé thick wall: σ_θ(a) = p (b² + a²)/(b² − a²); von Mises stress at the bore √3 p b²/(b² − a²)

Fully plastic or compound wall: p = (2/√3) σ_y ln(b/a)
Rail launcher: F = L′I²/2. Coil launcher and fusion coil: P = B²/(2μ₀)
Mass driver: a = P/(ρL), length = v²/(2a), with P capped by the strength of the payload
limits: A static, long, homogeneous cylinder with isotropic yield criteria. Fibre laminates are only screened for transverse compression at the bore.
Lamé statics holds when the pulse is longer than about three hoop acoustic transits. Shorter pulses are flagged as inertial.
No thermal, fatigue or end effects.
